findings.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — Severity P1, confidence 100, wrong-shape advisory: the verbatim code `b.cacheMu.Lock(); b.cache[key] = idx; b.cacheMu.Unlock()` protects only publication, not the get/build/publish transition, so two concurrent first lookups for the same uncached key build separate indexes; when the first index is published and receives a watch update before the second stale snapshot is published, the second assignment definitively discards that update and all later searches return stale data (and two file-backed builds contend for the same directory); the trigger is concurrent lazy lookup of one key, the consequence is duplicate full scans followed by stale search state or a failed lookup, and the affected parties are search clients and storage operators; the strongest rebuttal is that startup stats contain unique keys and the map write itself is locked, but that fails because `getOrCreateIndex` is also called concurrently by requests and watch processing, and map safety does not make the per-key lifecycle atomic.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:190 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, info.NamespacedResource, info.Count, info.ResourceVersion); return err` stores every parallel worker result in the same captured `err`; after `BuildIndex` was unlocked to make workers run concurrently, a successful worker can overwrite another worker's failure before that goroutine evaluates `return err`, so `group.Wait()` definitively reports success with an initial index missing and the server starts with incomplete search coverage.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — Severity P2, confidence 100, wrong-shape advisory: the verbatim code `err := s.Init(ctx)` makes object construction synchronously call backend lifecycle initialization, enumerate every namespaced resource, materialize every index above `InitMinCount`, and start watches before returning; the trigger is any deployment with search enabled, the consequence is constructor latency and readiness scaling with the entire stored dataset while even health service registration waits, and the affected parties are all clients and operators during startup; the strongest rebuttal is that eager initialization removes first-request latency and guarantees a ready server, but that fails because small indexes remain lazy by design and full-dataset materialization belongs to an explicit cancellable startup/readiness phase rather than a constructor with no context parameter.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:229 — Severity P2, confidence 100, coupling advisory: the verbatim code `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(claims.WithClaims(context.Background(),` is now the context passed by the constructor to `s.Init(ctx)`, coupling backend initialization and index population to an internally rooted service-account context; the trigger is shutdown or startup cancellation while indexing is in progress, the consequence is that callers cannot cancel the work because `cancel` is reachable only through `Stop` on the server that has not yet been returned, and the affected parties are process lifecycle managers and operators whose graceful shutdown deadline is consumed by the scan; the strongest rebuttal is that the context is cancellable and `Stop` calls `s.cancel()`, but that fails because no caller can invoke `Stop` until `NewResourceServer` completes.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:294 — Severity P3, confidence 100, simplification advisory: the verbatim code `s.once.Do(func() {` preserves a lazy-initialization state machine after line 258 made initialization an unconditional constructor step; the trigger is every successful construction, the consequence is ambiguous dual ownership of initialization and dead synchronization complexity for maintainers, and the affected parties are server integrators and future lifecycle-hook authors; specifically `once sync.Once` at line 288 and the `s.once.Do` wrapper at lines 294–316 are unnecessary because the returned `ResourceServer` interface does not expose `Init` and the repository has no remaining call site beyond the constructor; the strongest rebuttal is that retaining `sync.Once` preserves compatibility for possible direct concrete callers, but that fails because the constructor returns only the interface and keeping an unreachable second lifecycle entry point obscures rather than preserves the changed contract.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:297 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `if idx == nil { idx, _, err = s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0) }` has no per-key single-flight after the Bleve global build lock was removed, so concurrent first searches for the same uncached file-backed key both call `bleve.New` for the same directory and one request fails instead of sharing the completed index.

pkg/server/module_server_test.go:36 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.") }` disables the PostgreSQL execution of the only changed startup integration test, so constructor-time initialization regressions on that supported backend pass CI without verification.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:1 — Severity P2, confidence 100: the verbatim requirement `# Task: Unified Storage Performance Optimizations` defines no latency, throughput, concurrency, or startup-cost acceptance criterion and the diff adds no benchmark, so the task can be declared complete even when the changed initialization and index-build paths are slower than the baseline.

docs/metareview/reviews/mrv-20260911-014529341243000-task-done-task-001-430cbac4.md:50 — Severity P2, confidence 100: the verbatim recommendation `metareview fsm --workflow review-loop --base <ref>` supplies no FSM subcommand, so metareview 0.11.1 deterministically returns `unknown subcommand --workflow` and an author following the prescribed subagent-review remediation cannot create the required adjudicated review record.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:303 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim ordering `s.initErr = s.search.init(ctx)` before `s.initErr = s.initWatcher()` creates a silent event-loss window: when another server writes to the shared backend while the full search initialization is running, the later server watcher calls `WatchWriteEvents`, whose SQL implementation initializes its cursor from the then-latest resource versions, so that committed event is permanently skipped and a client resuming from an earlier resource version never receives it; the trigger is an HA/external write during startup indexing, the consequence is an incomplete watch stream, and the affected parties are watch clients and controllers; the strongest rebuttal is that no local client can watch before construction finishes, but that fails because the backend explicitly supports HA writes and clients resume from previously issued versions, while the search watch is a separate consumer that never feeds `s.broadcaster`.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:190 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, info.NamespacedResource, info.Count, info.ResourceVersion); return err` writes and reads one captured `err` from every parallel initialization worker; now that Bleve no longer serializes the whole build, when a successful worker overwrites `err` between a failing worker's assignment and return, `group.Wait()` receives nil for that failed build and `NewResourceServer` reports success with an index missing, so search users get invisible partial initialization; the strongest rebuttal is that `errgroup` captures each callback's error, but that fails because each callback returns the shared variable rather than a local build error.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `b.cacheMu.Lock(); b.cache[key] = idx; b.cacheMu.Unlock()` locks only publication after `builder(idx)` has already performed a full storage scan, so concurrent first searches for the same uncached key all build in parallel; this creates unbounded request-path amplification of full `ListIterator` queries, file-backed builds contend for the same directory, and for memory indexes a watch update applied to the first published index is definitively discarded when a later stale build overwrites the cache; the trigger is concurrent cold-key lookup, the consequence is failed requests or silently stale search results, and the affected parties are search users and the shared database; the strongest rebuttal is that cache writes are locked, but that fails because map safety does not provide per-key single-flight or a cache recheck before the expensive build and overwrite.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — Severity P1, confidence 100, latent-fragility advisory: the verbatim code `err := s.Init(ctx)` synchronously performs database initialization, full index scans, and watcher setup using the `ctx` created by `context.WithCancel(claims.WithClaims(context.Background(),`; works today, breaks when a backend connect, ping, stats query, list, or watcher setup waits for context cancellation, because the constructor has no caller context or deadline and `cancel` is reachable only through `Stop` on the server that has not been returned, leaving process startup hung indefinitely; the trigger is a stalled outbound backend operation, the consequence is total service unavailability, and the affected parties are operators and all clients; the strongest rebuttal is that the context is cancellable, but that fails because no caller can invoke its cancel function until this blocking call returns.

pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:261 — Severity P2, confidence 100, latent-fragility advisory: the verbatim failure path `return nil, err` performs no cancellation or cleanup after partial eager initialization; works today, breaks when search initialization successfully starts its `watchctx := context.Background()` watcher and the subsequent server watcher initialization fails, because the constructor returns no server handle while the search goroutine and backend poller retain the server and continue forever, leaking polling, index work, and resources; the trigger is a transient failure opening the second watch, the consequence is an invisible orphaned subsystem despite construction reporting failure, and the affected parties are operators and the backend; the strongest rebuttal is that an unpublished server is garbage-collected, but that fails because the live background goroutines retain it and their background context is never canceled.

pkg/server/module_server_test.go:35 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `// TODO - fix this test for postgres` followed by `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.") }` is not traceable to the stated “Unified Storage Performance Optimizations” scope and causes the PostgreSQL instrumentation-server path to stop running in Drone, so regressions in that supported database path pass CI undetected; the strongest rebuttal is that the test fails only in Drone and works locally, but that fails because it concedes an unresolved environment-specific failure and supplies no performance requirement that authorizes suppressing the affected party’s PostgreSQL CI coverage.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:126 — P2, confidence 100: verbatim vulnerable code `_, err = builder(idx)` followed only after the full build by `b.cacheMu.Lock(); b.cache[key] = idx; b.cacheMu.Unlock()`. A caller can send concurrent `Search` requests for the same uncached namespaced resource; every request observes the cache miss and simultaneously performs the unbounded database scan/index build before any mutex is acquired, exhausting database connections, CPU, and memory and denying unified-storage service to all tenants. Strongest author rebuttal: startup prebuilds indexes with `WorkerThreads` limiting concurrency. It fails because `InitMinCount` intentionally leaves indexes lazy and runtime `getOrCreateIndex` has neither that worker limit nor a per-key lock/singleflight, so request concurrency directly determines build concurrency.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:146 — P2, confidence 75: verbatim vulnerable code `for _, v := range b.cache {` iterates the Go map without `cacheMu`, while the changed writer remains `b.cache[key] = idx`; the newly added startup call `s.search.TotalDocs()` executes after the search watch goroutine has started, so a write event for a not-yet-cached namespaced resource can insert during this iteration and terminate the process with Go's fatal `concurrent map iteration and map write`, denying service to every user. Strongest author rebuttal: `group.Wait()` means index construction is finished before `TotalDocs`. It fails because `search.go` starts the event goroutine before calling `TotalDocs`, and that goroutine invokes `getOrCreateIndex`/`BuildIndex` for new resource keys independently of the completed startup group.

pkg/server/module_server_test.go:63 — [blocking] P1; confidence 100; verbatim `assert.Equal(t, 200, res.StatusCode)`: this endpoint-status assertion cannot distinguish the new eager `NewResourceServer` initialization and search-before-watcher ordering from the old lazy initialization, and it never exercises concurrent Bleve index construction, so the diff's changed lifecycle and concurrency behavior can be wrong while the only modified test remains green; this is present-but-irrelevant test coverage and therefore false confidence.

pkg/server/module_server_test.go:36 — [advisory: coverage gap] P1; confidence 100; verbatim `if dbType == "postgres" { t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.") }`: whenever the PostgreSQL CI job selects this backend, execution exits before `InitializeModuleServer`, converting the known PostgreSQL startup failure into a successful skip and leaving PostgreSQL users exposed to an unverified eager-initialization path; the strongest author rebuttal is that this is a temporary quarantine for Drone instability, but it fails because the skip is unconditional for every PostgreSQL run, has no expiry or alternate PostgreSQL assertion, and suppresses the exact failing behavior instead of isolating infrastructure flakiness.

pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — [advisory: coverage gap] P2; confidence 100; verbatim `b.cacheMu.Lock(); b.cache[key] = idx; b.cacheMu.Unlock()`: moving the lock from the whole `BuildIndex` operation to cache publication creates a new concurrent same-key lifecycle that the modified HTTP metrics test never invokes; two callers can both run the builder and publish different indexes, so search callers and index metrics observe duplicate work or different index instances, affecting storage/search users and maintainers; the strongest author rebuttal is that `searchSupport` prevents duplicate same-key builds, but it fails because `getOrCreateIndex` performs an unlocked `GetIndex`-then-`BuildIndex` sequence and its own comment explicitly says same-key builds need coordination.

pkg/server/module_server_test.go:36 — [advisory: fragile test structure] P2; confidence 100; verbatim `t.Skip("skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.")`: the test outcome is controlled by an ambient backend string and permanently skips the backend with the known failure, so CI stays green when that failure changes, worsens, or is fixed and later regresses, leaving PostgreSQL users and CI maintainers without a stable signal; the strongest author rebuttal is that backend-specific skipping avoids a flaky job, but it fails because this is a blanket backend exclusion rather than a bounded flaky-condition check and the package contains no replacement PostgreSQL test.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `_, _, err = s.build(...)` stores results in a 'captured err' variable that gets overwritten by parallel workers. However, looking at the diff, the code at line 190 shows `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, info.NamespacedResource, info.Count, info.ResourceVersion)` followed by `return err`. This is inside a function passed to `group.Go()` from errgroup. In Go's errgroup, each goroutine's function returns its own error independently - the `err` variable is local to each anonymous function closure, not shared. The errgroup.Wait() collects the first non-nil error from any goroutine. The finding misunderstands how errgroup and Go closures work - each goroutine has its own `err` variable in its scope, they don't share a single `err` variable that could be overwritten.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:258 — Severity P2, confidence 100, wrong-shape advisory: the verbatim code `err := s.Init(ctx)` makes object construction synchronously call backend lifecycle initialization, enumerate every namespaced resource, materialize every index above `InitMinCount`, and start watches before returning; the trigger is any deployment with search enabled, the consequence is constructor latency and readiness scaling with the entire stored dataset while even health service registration waits, and the affected parties are all clients and operators during startup; the strongest rebuttal is that eager initialization removes first-request latency and guarantees a ready server, but that fails because small indexes remain lazy by design and full-dataset materialization belongs to an explicit cancellable startup/readiness phase rather than a constructor with no context parameter.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the diff moves `s.Init(ctx)` into `NewResourceServer()` constructor (line 258), making initialization synchronous during object construction. The diff shows Init() calls `s.search.init(ctx)` which initializes search indexes, and `s.initWatcher()`. Previously, Init() was called lazily on each request (the diff removes multiple `s.Init(ctx)` calls from Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob methods). This is a legitimate architectural concern - moving potentially expensive initialization into the constructor changes startup behavior. However, this is a design decision rather than a bug - the code will work correctly, just with different startup characteristics. The finding raises a valid scope/architecture concern about constructor latency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:229 — Severity P2, confidence 100, coupling advisory: the verbatim code `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(claims.WithClaims(context.Background(),` is now the context passed by the constructor to `s.Init(ctx)`, coupling backend initialization and index population to an internally rooted service-account context; the trigger is shutdown or startup cancellation while indexing is in progress, the consequence is that callers cannot cancel the work because `cancel` is reachable only through `Stop` on the server that has not yet been returned, and the affected parties are process lifecycle managers and operators whose graceful shutdown deadline is consumed by the scan; the strongest rebuttal is that the context is cancellable and `Stop` calls `s.cancel()`, but that fails because no caller can invoke `Stop` until `NewResourceServer` completes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `s.Init(ctx)` is now called inside `NewResourceServer` at line 258-261, before the server is returned. Looking at the context creation around line 229 (referenced in the finding), the context is created with `context.WithCancel(claims.WithClaims(context.Background(), ...))` and the cancel function is stored in `s.cancel`. The finding correctly identifies that if `Init` blocks (e.g., during index initialization which the diff shows happens synchronously via `s.search.init(ctx)`), there's no way for external callers to cancel this work since `Stop()` (which calls `s.cancel()`) cannot be invoked until `NewResourceServer` returns. This is a real architectural issue introduced by moving `Init` from lazy per-request calls to eager initialization in the constructor.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the diff moves initialization from lazy (via s.once.Do in each method) to eager (in NewResourceServer constructor at lines 255-260). The s.once.Do wrapper at line 294 is now only called once from the constructor, making the sync.Once mechanism redundant. The diff shows Init() calls being removed from Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, and GetBlob methods. Since Init is now called unconditionally in the constructor and the interface doesn't expose Init, the sync.Once is indeed unnecessary complexity. This is a valid simplification advisory - not a bug, but a legitimate code quality concern about dead synchronization code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:297 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `if idx == nil { idx, _, err = s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0) }` has no per-key single-flight after the Bleve global build lock was removed, so concurrent first searches for the same uncached file-backed key both call `bleve.New` for the same directory and one request fails instead of sharing the completed index.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in bleve.go, the lock `b.cacheMu.Lock()` was moved from the beginning of BuildIndex to after the index is built (lines 88-89 removed, lines 137-139 added). This means the cache lookup and index building are no longer protected by the lock. In search.go line 297 (in getOrCreateIndex), there's a pattern `if idx == nil { idx, _, err = s.build(...) }` that checks the cache and builds if missing. Without the global lock during build, two concurrent requests for the same uncached key could both see idx==nil, both call build(), and both attempt bleve.New() on the same directory, causing a race condition where one fails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/resource/server.go:303 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim ordering `s.initErr = s.search.init(ctx)` before `s.initErr = s.initWatcher()` creates a silent event-loss window: when another server writes to the shared backend while the full search initialization is running, the later server watcher calls `WatchWriteEvents`, whose SQL implementation initializes its cursor from the then-latest resource versions, so that committed event is permanently skipped and a client resuming from an earlier resource version never receives it; the trigger is an HA/external write during startup indexing, the consequence is an incomplete watch stream, and the affected parties are watch clients and controllers; the strongest rebuttal is that no local client can watch before construction finishes, but that fails because the backend explicitly supports HA writes and clients resume from previously issued versions, while the search watch is a separate consumer that never feeds `s.broadcaster`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that reordering search.init() before initWatcher() creates an event-loss window. However, examining the diff: (1) The old code had initWatcher() before search.init(), and the new code reverses this order. (2) The finding's claim about 'silent event-loss window' assumes that events written during search initialization would be missed by the watcher. But the watcher initialization (initWatcher) happens AFTER search.init completes, so the watcher would start from the current resource version at that point. (3) The finding mentions 'HA/external write during startup' but this is speculative about external system behavior not shown in the diff. (4) The search index initialization and the watcher are separate concerns - the search index builds from existing data while the watcher handles new events. The reordering actually makes more sense: build the search index first from existing data, then start watching for new events. The finding's reasoning about event loss is not verifiable from the diff and appears to misunderstand the initialization flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:137 — Severity P1, confidence 100: the verbatim code `b.cacheMu.Lock(); b.cache[key] = idx; b.cacheMu.Unlock()` locks only publication after `builder(idx)` has already performed a full storage scan, so concurrent first searches for the same uncached key all build in parallel; this creates unbounded request-path amplification of full `ListIterator` queries, file-backed builds contend for the same directory, and for memory indexes a watch update applied to the first published index is definitively discarded when a later stale build overwrites the cache; the trigger is concurrent cold-key lookup, the consequence is failed requests or silently stale search results, and the affected parties are search users and the shared database; the strongest rebuttal is that cache writes are locked, but that fails because map safety does not provide per-key single-flight or a cache recheck before the expensive build and overwrite.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the lock was moved from before the builder call to after it. Previously, `b.cacheMu.Lock()` was at the start of BuildIndex (before the expensive builder operation), but now it only wraps the cache assignment at lines 137-139. This means multiple concurrent calls for the same uncached key will all execute the expensive `builder(idx)` function in parallel, then race to write to the cache. The last one to complete will overwrite earlier entries, potentially discarding updates that were applied to indexes built earlier. This is a real concurrency bug - the lock no longer provides single-flight semantics for index building, only for the final map write.
